science.title: Multi-scale evolution characteristics of coal low temperature oxidation under varying water content and the promotion-inhibition coupling mechanism of spontaneous combustion
science.description: External water significantly influences the spontaneous combustion of goaf residual coal. To clarify the relationship between water content and combustion behavior, coal samples with water contents of 3%, 6.15%, 9.25%, 12.7%, and 16.89% were investigated using microstructural characterization, thermophysical measurements, and temperature-programmed oxidation. Oxygen adsorption capacity, specific surface area (SSA), functional groups, thermophysical properties, and oxidation behavior were systematically analyzed. Oxygen adsorption reached a maximum at 6.15% water content. At 30 °C, SSA decreases from 2.43 m2·g− 1 to 1.35 m2·g− 1 with increasing water content, whereas heating promoted pore development in high water content coal due to water removal. Higher water content increased the contents of –OH, C = O, and –COOH while decreasing C = C and C–O. Increasing water content also enhanced specific heat capacity but reduced thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity, weakening heat transfer within coal. Gas generation, oxygen consumption, and heat release exhibited bell-shaped trends with maxima at 6.15% moisture. For example, at 160 °C, the oxygen consumption at 6.15% water content is approximately 49.6% higher than that at 16.89%, while the CO and CO2 yields follow an identical rank order of 6.15%>9.25%>12.7%>3%>16.89% across the oxidation stages. The apparent activation energy reached minimum values of 33.41 and 49.55 kJ·mol− 1 in Stages I and II, respectively, at 6.15% water content, then increased by 21.9% and 22.0% at 16.89%, indicating that excessive water suppresses low-temperature oxidation. These findings provide theoretical support for preventing spontaneous combustion of water-immersed residual coal in goaf.

science.title: Pyrimidine derivatives with cholinesterase inhibitory, anticonvulsant, and anticancer activities evaluated through experimental and computational studies
science.description: A series of pyrimidine derivatives (1–12) was synthesized and investigated as multifunctional bioactive molecules based on their promising molecular docking profiles against cholinesterase targets, which provided the rationale for subsequent biological evaluation. The synthesized compounds were evaluated for acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE) inhibition, anticonvulsant activity, anticancer potential, and computational characteristics. Among the tested compounds, compound 4 exhibited the highest cholinesterase inhibitory activity with IC50 values of 0.70 ± 0.03 µM (AChE) and 2.90 ± 0.12 µM (BChE), while compounds 1, 2, 9, and 11 also showed potent dual enzyme inhibition (AChE IC50 = 0.95–1.60 µM; BChE IC50 = 3.60–4.20 µM). In vivo anticonvulsant studies demonstrated that compound 4 produced the greatest seizure protection, achieving 83% protection in the maximal electroshock seizure (MES) model and 85% protection in the pentylenetetrazole (PTZ) model at 20 mg/kg, whereas compounds 1, 2, 9, and 11 also exhibited pronounced dose-dependent anticonvulsant effects. In cytotoxicity studies, compounds 2 and 11 displayed selective antiproliferative activity against SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells with IC50 values of 45.6 and 46.3 µM, respectively, while exhibiting comparatively low toxicity toward normal neuronal cells. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable binding of the lead compounds within the active sites of AChE and BChE through multiple hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic interactions, supporting the observed experimental activities. Hence, the combined computational and experimental findings identify compounds 2, 4, and 11 as promising lead pyrimidine derivatives for further optimization as multifunctional agents targeting cholinesterase-associated neurological disorders with additional selective anticancer potential.
